system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Buyer Response — Critical Review of Seller's Update Draft

I have reviewed the Seller's positions against the Project Kestrel playbook and find **substantive departures across nearly every major line**, not a "fair and balanced" package. Several of these are strategic moves designed to shrink our fallback position below the team's approved threshold while leaving the seller underfunded and unprotected. Below are the material departures and recommended pushes back.

---

## 1. General Warranty Cap

**Seller:** AGREES unconditionally to a 20% cap (AUD 4,800,000) and nothing more.

**Playbook:** Starting position of **AUD 6,000,000 (25%)**, with a 20%/AUD 4,800,000 fallback *only* upon prior written authority from our principal, Amelia Frost, identifying the draft. No such authority has been given.

**Why it matters:** The seller has knifed the baseline cap to bare floor while disclaiming any formalisation pathway. If we surrender here, there is no mechanism to restore the 25% base later, meaning we permanently concede effective general-warranty coverage at AUD 4,800,000 unless future negotiate restore power.

**Push back:** Restore the starting position at 25% / AUD 6,000,000. Frame any acceptance of a lower cap as contingent on Amelia Frost authorising the specific draft and deleting the language that would otherwise function as a non-derogable hard floor.

---

## 2. Thresholds

**Seller:** De minimis **AUD 25,000**; basket **AUD 250,000**, seller liable only above the basket.

**Playbook:** De minimis **AUD 5,000**; basket **AUD 50,000**, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.

**Why it matters:** Both thresholds are far higher on every comparable dollar basis. Raising the de minimis from AUD 5,000 to AUD 25,000 collapses the effective scope of any claim below AUD 25,000, meaning small and medium claims are instantly forfeited by definition. Raising the basket from AUD 50,000 to AUD 250,000 means roughly five times the volume of claims sits inside the partial-liability zone. The math asymmetry is the strongest signal that the seller intends to preclude recovering material amounts regardless of where a claim falls inside the bracket.

**Push back:** Demand the playbook thresholds retroactively: de minimis AUD 5,000, basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded. Do not allow any redefinition. If the parties want baskets, a meaningful calibration argument is that the buyer is buying from the seller's own books and may encounter slippage — reject as structured above.

---

## 3. Time Limits — Scope Capture

**Seller:** General claims at 18 months; *"any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."*

**Playbook:** General claims period is 24 months after Completion as standard; 18 months fallback **requires** written approval from Amelia Frost (none given). Fundamental / Title claims operate under a separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge constructs.

**Why it matters:** The seller has captured title and capacity warranties inside the 18-month limitation shoehorn, removing the structural separation the playbook requires. "Unless expressly stated otherwise" is a blunt instrument — it gives the seller permission to lock title claims into the general basket, risking the 100%-cap, six-year regime we need to survive independently.

**Push back:** Delete the broad catch-all escape clause. Require that Limitation, Exclusivity, and Non-Reliance apply to general claims only; explicitly exempt Fundamental and Title claims from general caps, baskets, knowledge bars and time limits. Confirm title is investigated independently and covered regardless of general-claim windows.

---

## 4. Fraud, Wilful Concealment & Deliberate Misconduct

**Seller:** No specific assurance of carve-out here. The broad scope capture noted in point 3 risks sweeping fraud carve-outs into the general limiter language rather than preserving them.

**Playbook:** Carve-out must apply to all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, enforceable at maximum extent, and **no one may waive it**.

**Why it matters:** Ambiguity here is a procurement-risk vector. Where fraud exists, the seller will attempt to position the general 18-month window or 20% basket as closing it off; absent an explicit, enforceable carve-out the seller can argue the carve-out doesn't apply because the relevant limitation clause covers it.

**Push back:** Insert an explicit, express clause confirming fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct are carved out of every cap, basket, threshold, claim period, exclusive remedy, non-reliance and knowledge provision. Cross-reference to Section 9.3 and delete any blanket disclaimer language. Require the Seller to sign the carve-out without waiver language.

---

## 5. Disclosure

**Seller:** General disclosure of the full data room, Accounts, statutory registers, and publicly searchable corporate records (deemed whole-data-room); Schedule 7 mirrors this via general disclosure.

**Playbook:** Require specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

**Why it matters:** The seller is offering de facto deemed disclosure — every file in the room, every searchable record — which defeats the point of information rooms and creates hindsight-based claim risks for the buyer.

**Push back:** Redefine Schedule 7 to enumerate specific disclosures item by item (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, employee bonuses, export, title, supplier renewals, Mossvale, office lease). Delete general-disclosure and public-register language. Require each disclosure to be signed and accompanied by confirmatory evidence from the respective data room file within defined dates.

---

## 6. Buyer Knowledge

**Seller:** Clause 8.3 — Buyer has **no claim** on any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including discoverable from the data room or public records.

**Playbook:** Delete the blanket exclusion; any qualifier requires named seller knowledge persons plus reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud, or a specific indemnity.

**Why it matters:** This is the most direct paragraph-level departure. A blanket data-room/public-records excluder effectively makes entire transaction components "seller knowledge," closing buyer exposure on matters the buyer couldn't reasonably have known about. Combined with a higher de minimis, this synergistically packs the exclusion net much tighter than the buyer wants.

**Push back:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely and substitute a bright-line requirement: any buyer-knowledge exclusion must name the specific seller person(s) involved, state the nature of knowledge, and require a reasonable enquiry standard. Maintain title and capacity warranties unaffected by knowledge bars.

---

## 7. Bluefen Change-Control Consent

**Seller:** Consent treated as satisfied on delivery of counterparty's written consent; conditions in 11.2–11.3 not addressed. DD-002 confirms no final written consent included, no
